Cadence has beaten EPS estimates five straight quarters yet averaged a -0.69% post-earnings stock move, with 23 analysts maintaining Buy or Strong Buy ratings.

CEO Anirudh Devgan called the Intel 14A agreement "100% additional," but hardware remains supply-constrained and guidance assumes export controls stay "substantially similar."

Cadence's record $8.10B backlog and 24% revenue growth last quarter haven't prevented shares from sitting well below their 52-week high at 64 times earnings.

Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor)

Cadence Design Systems (NASDAQ:CDNS) is expected to report third-quarter results Monday, October 26, after the close. The stock is up only 0.61% year to date, so this report needs to justify a premium multiple.

HelloRF Zcool / Shutterstock.com
Record Backlog Meets a Stalled Stock

Last quarter, revenue rose 24.2% to $1.584B, and non-GAAP EPS of $2.11 beat the $2.06 estimate. Non-GAAP operating margin expanded to 45.5% from 42.8%, and backlog reached a record $8.10B. Management raised full-year revenue guidance to $6.26B to $6.34B.

Growth was broad. Core EDA grew 18%, Semiconductor IP 40%, and System Design and Analysis 37% with help from the Hexagon D&E deal.

Shares have fell behind anyway. At $314.48, the stock is down 5.69% over the past year and well below its $416.69 52-week high. It still trades at 64 times trailing earnings and 32 times forward earnings.

The upside depends on three catalysts: the Intel 18A ramp, accelerating Data Center and AI demand, and a foundry business that can win outside customers. If all three deliver, the recent pullback would sit within a real turnaround.

Intel Gave Back 14% in a Month Despite Record Growth

Intel shares have fallen 8.31% over the past week and 14.43% over the past month. Still, the stock is up 151.84% year to date and stands about 34.7% below its 52-week high of $142.35.

On Monday, JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM), a longtime bear, upgraded Intel to neutral from underweight. Intel's third-quarter report is expected after the close on October 29.

The last earnings report was strong. Q2 revenue came in at $16.13 billion (+25.4% YoY), ahead of estimates for $14.45 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.42 exceeded the $0.22 consensus. CEO Lip-Bu Tan called it the "strongest revenue growth in more than fifteen years."

title: Intel (INTC) Stock Looks Rich Against Its Cash Flow Recovery Story
detail:
Intel (INTC) Stock Looks Rich Against Its Cash Flow Recovery Story
Bailey Pemberton
Thu, October 22, 2026 at 7:12 AM MST 4 min read
INTC
Trade Intel on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Intel has produced huge returns over the past few years, even as headlines swing between AI optimism, funding concerns, and sector-wide selloffs. With the stock last closing at US$92.96, the question for you now is whether that price still lines up with the cash flows the business can realistically generate.

Intel has delivered a 3 year share price gain of 187.9%, which puts a lot of weight on the idea that its future cash flows can support a much larger equity value than a few years ago.

Heavy spending on foundry capacity, new AI focused GPUs and data center products, plus fresh equity raises, can reshape both Intel's long term cash generation and the timing of when free cash flow turns more supportive for shareholders.

Prefer to judge Intel on sales? See why Intel's 8.6x P/S tells a different valuation story.

The issue now is whether Intel's current valuation is justified by the cash flows implied by a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) view over the next few years.

If you want to test the same cash flow question you are asking of Intel across a wider field of AI focused chip players, scan through 55 AI infrastructure stocks.

Has Intel Run Too Far on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model here asks whether Intel's future cash generation can justify today's US$92.96 share price. On recent numbers the picture is still in rebuild mode. The latest twelve month free cash flow shows an outflow of about US$4.8b, so the model leans heavily on a recovery story rather than steady surplus cash today.

Analysts and extrapolated estimates in this DCF point to free cash flow shifting into positive territory and then growing through the early 2030s. This helps explain why the valuation still implies recovering cash flows despite that recent drag. Intel's heavy spend on foundry buildouts and AI infrastructure is central here, since the projections assume those investments eventually support much larger yearly cash inflows for equity holders. The recent sector wide selloff in semiconductor and AI related stocks helps explain why the DCF outcome now sits meaningfully below the market price instead of lining up more closely.
